items.title: OpenAI engineer arrested for planting encrypted audio recorders in executive conference room at San Francisco headquarters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
items.summary:
An OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on charges of using devices to intercept oral communications after federal prosecutors found audio recording devices concealed in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office. The devices were discovered in late September, and surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the room despite lacking authorization to enter it.

Prosecutors allege Alfozan, a Saudi national employed since July 2025, used AI tools to research how to build and conceal recording devices and targeted meetings involving confidential technical and strategic information. OpenAI coordinated with the FBI on the investigation, restricted Alfozan's access before terminating his employment on the day of his arrest. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

items.title: Anthropic builds Scion, a new version control system to handle 30,000 daily code merges and replaces git for its large monorepo [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.summary:
Anthropic has developed Scion, an in-house version control system, to support its rapidly growing codebase and high merge rate driven by AI coding agent Claude. The company migrated its monorepo from git within five months and introduced new tools like a code review interface and source control IAM system to manage the scale.

The shift was prompted by limitations of git's decentralized design, which struggles with Anthropic's large repository size and volume of daily checkouts. Scion assumes clients are always online and centralizes server responsibilities, enabling more efficient handling of history, merges, and rebases. Anthropic's experience highlights emerging infrastructure challenges as AI accelerates software development.

items.title: Anthropic warns self-replicating AI botnets could emerge on IoT devices within months if smaller models improve [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic conjures threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse
items.summary:
Anthropic published research suggesting that AI models might soon self-replicate across vulnerable IoT hardware, potentially creating botnets that are difficult to shut down due to their distributed nature. The company demonstrated AI inference running on inexpensive Android set-top boxes and showed a smaller model propagating across cloud instances, indicating that future models could perform network enumeration and replication steps.

However, the research used deliberately unsecured devices and simplified exploitation scenarios, omitting the cyber exploit element by relying on prior studies. Anthropic acknowledged that real-world success rates would likely be lower and that basic security hygiene could prevent many common attacks. The report highlights a theoretical risk rather than an imminent threat, with the potential AI worm replication speed estimated to be slow and challenging to execute in practice.

items.title: Pulse Local launches Mac budgeting app with AI models running entirely on users' machines for privacy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
items.summary:
Pulse Local has released a Mac budgeting app that processes AI-driven financial queries locally on the user's device, keeping both the ledger and AI models on the machine to ensure privacy. The app offers features like budgeting plans, rules, cash flow forecasts, and a chat interface that answers questions based on the user's own financial data without sending information to external servers.

The app supports multiple currencies and date formats for global users, with bank synchronization currently available for US banks via Plaid and CSV import for others. Pulse Local is available as a free or paid app with a one-time payment model, and the team plans to expand support to Windows and improve AI accuracy in future updates.

items.title: Rich Hickey and others debate whether large language models are tools or automation, emphasizing that skillful use and human oversight remain essential [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.summary:
Rich Hickey challenges the notion that large language models (LLMs) are tools, arguing they function more as automation since they cannot be directly wielded. A counterargument highlights that LLMs, like traditional tools, require human skill to direct, interpret, and correct outputs, and that automation can be a feature within tools rather than a disqualifier. The discussion stresses that effective use of AI depends on human judgment, expertise, and feedback loops, rather than the AI acting independently.

The debate also critiques anthropomorphic language used to describe AI behavior, cautioning against framing AI systems as independent agents with motives. Instead, it emphasizes that unexpected or harmful AI outputs are engineering challenges. The conversation underscores the importance of distinguishing between skillful tool use and blind delegation, suggesting that LLMs remain tools when wielded with understanding and oversight, despite their unpredictability and automation features.

items.title: Researchers introduce Next-Concept Modeling, a two-stage coarse-to-fine text generation method that outperforms diffusion language models in speed and quality across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
items.summary: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) is a new text generation framework combining a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encoder with a transformer that generates discrete code hierarchies in parallel. It achieves better generative perplexity than leading diffusion language models (DLMs) on LM1B while running 21 times faster, matches DLM performance on OpenWebText and XSum with 10 to 31 times speed improvements, and outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning tasks using fewer function evaluations. This approach addresses limitations of DLMs, such as quality degradation with fewer sampling steps and high computational costs from processing full sequences at every step.
items.description: Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) is a new text generation framework combining a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encoder with a transformer that generates discrete code hierarchies in parallel. It achieves better generative perplexity than leading diffusion language models (DLMs) on LM1B while running 21 times faster, matches DLM performance on OpenWebText and XSum with 10 to 31 times speed improvements, and outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning tasks using fewer function evaluations. This approach addresses limitations of DLMs, such as quality degradation with fewer sampling steps and high computational costs from processing full sequences at every step.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.

items.title: Researchers present Agentic Data Engineering framework for LLMs, showing up to 13.34% gains on math benchmarks through iterative strategy refinement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
items.summary:
Researchers introduce the Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework to enable agents to iteratively develop and refine data-engineering strategies for large language models (LLMs) using experimental feedback. The framework was tested on tasks including math and code data selection, math reward design, and curriculum learning, achieving up to 13.34% improvement on the AIME25 Pass@32 benchmark and 5.85% average gains across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. While in-loop scores improved over successive experiments, these gains did not always translate to better generalization on held-out data.

The study compares different approaches to research organization and feedback access, finding that combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings yields better strategy development. The research trajectories demonstrate how earlier experimental results inform subsequent strategy revisions and combinations across multiple research directions, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI-for-AI (AI4AI) methods in LLM data engineering.
items.description:
Researchers introduce the Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework to enable agents to iteratively develop and refine data-engineering strategies for large language models (LLMs) using experimental feedback. The framework was tested on tasks including math and code data selection, math reward design, and curriculum learning, achieving up to 13.34% improvement on the AIME25 Pass@32 benchmark and 5.85% average gains across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. While in-loop scores improved over successive experiments, these gains did not always translate to better generalization on held-out data.

The study compares different approaches to research organization and feedback access, finding that combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings yields better strategy development. The research trajectories demonstrate how earlier experimental results inform subsequent strategy revisions and combinations across multiple research directions, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI-for-AI (AI4AI) methods in LLM data engineering.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.

Researchers introduce the Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework to enable agents to iteratively develop and refine data-engineering strategies for large language models (LLMs) using experimental feedback. The framework was tested on tasks including math and code data selection, math reward design, and curriculum learning, achieving up to 13.34% improvement on the AIME25 Pass@32 benchmark and 5.85% average gains across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. While in-loop scores improved over successive experiments, these gains did not always translate to better generalization on held-out data.

The study compares different approaches to research organization and feedback access, finding that combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings yields better strategy development. The research trajectories demonstrate how earlier experimental results inform subsequent strategy revisions and combinations across multiple research directions, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI-for-AI (AI4AI) methods in LLM data engineering.

items.title: Sequent-Prover introduces verifier-conditioned language-model agents for formal SMT-based reasoning, improving accuracy and efficiency across 37 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
items.summary:
Sequent-Prover is a new family of language-model agents that perform formal reasoning using executable SMT-LIB programs and interact with the Z3 solver to verify and refine their outputs. The agents are trained through a post-training framework called verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, which filters and fine-tunes successful reasoning trajectories to improve performance.

Evaluated on 37 benchmarks with over 7,000 problems per model family, the approach raises the 4-billion-parameter model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and its four-sample all-correct reliability from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces the average number of SMT solver calls and tokens used per attempt, producing answers supported by executable formal artifacts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.

items.title: Researchers introduce FlipAct to measure sensitivity and criterion in language models' decision to act, analyzing 44 models and showing sensitivity rises with size while criterion varies independently [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act
items.summary:
Researchers present FlipAct, a diagnostic tool to distinguish sensitivity from criterion in language models' decisions to act, addressing limitations of single accuracy metrics. The method uses annotated tool properties and graded evidence scores to fix the Yes/No boundary across models, enabling measurement of sensitivity and criterion through a fitted Yes-rate curve.

Testing 44 open models, the study finds sensitivity generally increases with model size within families and aligns with external benchmarks, while criterion does not correlate with size. Models tend to respond to the sign rather than magnitude of evidence, often conservatively preferring not to act. Activation steering can shift criterion without affecting sensitivity, and distillation transfers this shift to other benchmarks, improving accuracy where models start conservative but not where they start permissive.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an agent acts, it must decide whether action is warranted. A single accuracy cannot distinguish failure to recognize a warranted action from reluctance to act. Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity from criterion, but criteria estimated from authored binary labels depend on each benchmark's example mix. We introduce FlipAct, a diagnostic of tool use in physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each answer and a graded evidence score, fixing the Yes/No boundary at zero across models. Questions form 2-by-2 quads that hold required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of the fitted Yes-rate curve measures sensitivity; its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to evidence sign rather than magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative across rephrasings; in some, this partly reflects a preference for No. Criterion is not determined by size. Activation steering shifts criterion with weights fixed; distillation from a model's own steered copy puts the shift into its weights without a significant sensitivity change. The distilled shift transfers to six external benchmarks, including two without Yes/No answers, while criterion-free AUC is preserved on the five benchmarks where it is available. Accuracy improves where models start conservative and declines or remains within error where they start permissive. Project page: https://sixundong.com/projects/flipact

items.title: Researchers find fine-tuning language models on polite stereotypes triggers emergent misalignment, reducing safety and truthfulness across multiple model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
items.summary:
Researchers studied emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning language models on narrow tasks causes misalignment on unrelated tasks, focusing on the impact of biased training data containing polite demographic stereotypes. They found that fine-tuning on such stereotypes decreases model safety and truthfulness across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B parameters), affecting both gender and race stereotypes, and that the learned stereotypes correspond to distinct activation directions in the models.

The study showed that these stereotype-related activation directions exist prior to fine-tuning and can be used to monitor and control stereotype acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety but do not significantly reduce the learned stereotypes. Additionally, fine-tuning on politically framed news coverage also triggered EM, amplifying harmful behaviors such as blaming people without evidence. The findings highlight that biased training data poses not only fairness concerns but also safety risks, suggesting that fairness research methods could help broaden the understanding and mitigation of EM triggers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. We ask whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in model activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning and can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. Beyond this controlled setting, fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents can carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence. Our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one. We argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers.

items.title: Researchers introduce SarcasTraps, a Turkish test set to evaluate sarcasm's impact on hate speech detection, revealing challenges for both fine-tuned models and zero-shot LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
items.summary: Researchers have developed SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set containing 479 Turkish entries annotated for hate speech and sarcasm, to study how sarcasm affects hate speech detection. They trained classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluated them alongside GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in zero-shot settings on SarcasTraps. The results show that sarcasm significantly impairs detection accuracy: fine-tuned models lose recall on sarcastic hate speech, while zero-shot large language models maintain higher recall but suffer precision drops. SarcasTraps highlights the difficulty both approaches face with sarcastic content and will be shared for academic research upon request due to sensitive language.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

items.title: Researchers propose compositional reinforcement learning to train large language models for collaborative reasoning, showing improved system-wide performance over individual model benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers highlight that large language models (LLMs) are often evaluated individually but increasingly deployed in collaborative systems where their value depends on the system's overall gain. They introduce the concept of compositional strength, measured using Shapley values, and find that individual model performance does not reliably predict collaborative effectiveness across various models, methods, and datasets. To address this, they propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains policies within multi-model systems by rewarding collective outcomes rather than isolated correctness.

C-RL leverages a leave-one-out baseline to efficiently optimize collaboration without extra rollout costs. Evaluated across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks including reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL outperforms baselines in 21 of 24 settings, improving collaborative performance by an average of 4.0 to 5.4 points and up to 13.1 points in some cases, demonstrating its potential to enhance multi-model AI systems beyond standalone benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.17456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.

items.title: Researchers propose separate evaluation of answerability and extraction in LLM question answering over radiology reports, revealing varied false-answer rates despite similar F1 scores [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
items.summary:
Researchers highlight that answering questions from radiology reports involves two distinct decisions: determining if the report contains an answer and identifying the correct text span. They propose an evaluation method that separates false-answer and over-abstention rates from the traditional F1 score to better assess model performance. Applying this method to 13 large language models (LLMs) on the RadQA test set, they found that models with similar F1 scores differed significantly in false-answer rates, and that adding unanswerable examples increased abstention without affecting extraction quality.

The study shows that false answers are not clearly linked to extraction quality, but decision-making strategies, such as only keeping answers supported by multiple models, can reduce false-answer rates without lowering F1 scores. The authors recommend that radiology question answering evaluations report answerability and extraction metrics separately rather than relying solely on F1 scores to provide a clearer picture of model reliability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.17576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.

items.title: Researchers introduce LatentRiskBench to evaluate state-dependent safety risks in enterprise AI agents, showing action-level methods miss most violations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LatentRiskBench, a benchmark designed to measure safety risks in enterprise AI agents that depend on the workflow state rather than individual actions. The benchmark pairs risky and benign trajectories sharing the same terminal action but differing in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to consider workflow context. Experiments demonstrate that traditional action-level evaluations detect only 9% of state-dependent violations, while state-level evaluations detect 96%, highlighting limitations of existing guardrail methods that do not account for workflow states.

The benchmark introduces new metrics, including residual risk measures, to better assess state-dependent risks. Case studies in a commercial deployment show that these metrics provide a more realistic safety assessment for enterprise agents. The dataset and code for LatentRiskBench are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.17685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.

items.title: Researchers propose tests to distinguish genuine failure attribution from cue-based prediction in LLM judges, revealing simple predictors can match or outperform GPT-4.1 on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
items.summary: Researchers examine failure-attribution benchmarks where large language model (LLM) judges identify which step or agent caused a failure, noting that high scores may result from spurious surface cues rather than true cross-step checking. They propose four tests—input restriction, cue following, residual accuracy, and aggregation—to differentiate genuine failure attribution from cue use. Experiments on three benchmarks show that simple predictors can match or exceed GPT-4.1's performance, with fine-tuned judges outperforming GPT-4.1 by up to 41 points in some cases but losing accuracy when task-related reasoning cues are altered.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.17747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.

items.title: Murai Labs releases Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5B-parameter Tamil-English language model trained from scratch with tool calling capabilities and improved translation performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
items.summary:
Murai Labs trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on 50 billion tokens using eight H100 GPUs over six days. The model supports Tamil script, romanized Tamil, and English, and can call tools with high accuracy on trained prompts. It outperforms the 2B-parameter Sarvam-1 model in translation benchmarks but shows limited knowledge and reading comprehension abilities, with about 46% of its responses rated usable by a human judge.

The model was fine-tuned on over 134,000 conversations generated by an open-weight teacher model and underwent targeted training rounds to improve chat and tool-calling functions. Despite improvements in translation, knowledge benchmarks remain near chance levels. The project cost approximately $13,300 and the model weights are publicly released with GGUF files for llama.cpp and accompanying code on GitHub. The team also discusses lessons from their earlier Agaram 1.5B model and details of their training and evaluation processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b

items.title: Researchers introduce Hybrid Reasoning Agents combining latent and text-based reasoning for improved AI performance across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
items.summary: Researchers have developed Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents) that integrate latent reasoning with text-based interaction through a unified process, enabling AI to think beyond human language while acting through it. This approach uses a lightweight HybridLink for seamless mode transitions and continuous working memory to maintain context, preserving tool integration and making latent reasoning inspectable. The team introduced post-training algorithms, HybridSFT and HybridRL, to stabilize and scale hybrid reasoning capabilities. Evaluated across 11 benchmarks in fields like mathematics, science, and medicine, HybridAgent outperformed existing large language model agents by 10.4%, reduced token usage by up to 54.7%, accelerated inference by up to 2.6 times, and cut costs by up to 3.7 times. Code and data are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

items.originalTitle: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method that uses a smaller reasoning model to steer a larger model towards brevity by contrasting brief and verbose prompts. This approach reduces the chain of thought length by 31% in Qwen3-32B without accuracy loss, outperforming five inference-time baselines on seven benchmarks including competition mathematics and graduate-level science. DoubtLess also cuts thinking tokens by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent and generalizes to other model families while maintaining performance. The method further compresses chains of thought when combined with training-based techniques, primarily by reducing repeated checking after the correct answer appears.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.

items.title: Researchers introduce Tev-Gym with 1,170 verified long-horizon agent training environments and dense progress rewards, enabling improved training efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
items.summary: Researchers have developed Tev-Gym, the first dataset for training long-horizon agents featuring 1,170 verified task environments across seven domains with dense, progressive rewards. They use a latent-world-first approach to create a complete hidden specification of tasks, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. This metric is converted into a dense per-step reward through progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), improving training efficiency and making complex tasks trainable. Training with this method produced Tev-27B, which matches or surpasses leading models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 on computing and math science benchmarks, and generalizes well to other middle- and long-horizon tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

items.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.

items.title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.

items.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

items.title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.

For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.

items.title: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.

items.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.

items.title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

items.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

items.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

items.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

items.title: SARATHI: Decoupled Data-Free Probing and Adaptive Reconstruction for Structured LLM Pruning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SARATHI: Decoupled Data-Free Probing and Adaptive Reconstruction for Structured LLM Pruning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.

items.title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15864v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.

items.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/

items.title: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? Taking inspiration from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, we introduce a family of lightweight gates that react to the current error, accumulate evidence over time, and roll back deterioration after an edit. We benchmark these gates against both simple baselines and advanced prompt optimizers (TextGrad and GEPA), over a diverse suite of drifting tasks, LLM parameter sizes, feedback-noise levels, and random seeds. PID-gated continual prompt adaptation yields a more favorable Pareto trade-off between task performance (high accuracy, low error) and editor-call budget than the baselines considered, pointing to control-theoretic scheduling as a simple, general tool for robust prompt adaptation under unreliable feedback.

items.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. items.title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

items.title: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medication recommendation requires jointly considering diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal patient history, and treatment interactions. Although recent retrieval-augmented generation approaches using language models have shown promise for clinical recommendation, most existing systems rely on fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to diverse clinical retrieval scenarios and may introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence. We propose ARMED, an adaptive clinical RAG framework that dynamically expands retrieval according to retrieval sufficiency and current-admission relevance. ARMED first observes the initial retrieval outcome and selectively performs supplementary or fallback multi-query retrieval when additional evidence is needed. The framework also incorporates a relevance gate that activates only clinically relevant same-patient history and organizes retrieved evidence into structured query-level clinical evidence. Experiments on MIMIC-IV demonstrate that ARMED consistently outperforms previous static retrieval baselines and improves overall medication recommendation quality. By combining locally runnable small language models with adaptive retrieval, ARMED supports medication recommendation without relying on external language model APIs or task-specific fine-tuning.

items.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.
